analysis.one_liner: Sets national limits on power plant sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, mercury, and carbon dioxide pollution through a cap-and-trade system.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill by Sen. Tom Carper to cap power plant pollution was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2007 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a national program limiting four pollutants from fossil-fuel power plants: sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide. It set declining caps starting in 2012, created a trading market for emissions allowances, and auctioned a growing share of those allowances, with the proceeds funding clean energy technology, energy efficiency, help for affected workers and communities, and wildlife protection. It also tightened standards for the oldest coal plants and barred new conventional coal plants from receiving carbon allowances.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near coal-fired power plants and downstream of acid rain would get cleaner air: national caps would force steep cuts in sulfur dioxide (to 2 million tons a year from 2015), nitrogen oxides, mercury (90% capture from 2015), and carbon dioxide. The auction proceeds would fund clean technology, energy efficiency, and adaptation assistance for workers, low-income energy consumers, and communities affected by climate change. Electric utilities would get something they asked for as well: a single, predictable national set of rules instead of piecemeal regulation.

how_it_helps.text: Sets national tonnage limits on sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide from power plants, with each excess ton treated as a separate violation [S2][S3].
Caps sulfur dioxide emissions at 2 million tons a year from 2015, splits nitrogen oxide caps between eastern and western states, and requires existing plants to capture 90% of mercury by 2015 [S3].
Caps carbon dioxide at 2006 levels for 2012-2014 and reduces the cap 1% to 1.5% a year thereafter, putting the power sector on a reduction path toward a 60-80% cut from current levels by 2050 [S3].

Auctions a growing share of emission allowances (18% in 2012 rising to 100% by 2036) and puts the proceeds into a Climate Action Trust Fund for clean and low-carbon technology, energy efficiency, research, adaptation assistance for displaced workers and low-income energy consumers, and fish and wildlife habitat protection [S3].

Starting in 2020, plants 40 or more years old that run more than 500 hours a year must meet modern performance standards for sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, closing part of the loophole that let aging coal plants run without modern controls [S2][S3].
Bars new coal-fired units that lack advanced clean coal technology from receiving carbon dioxide allowances, making it far harder to build conventional coal plants [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired power plants, which would bear compliance costs and lose the value of emitting freely; ultimately some of that cost would flow to electricity customers, particularly in coal-dependent regions. The coal mining industry would face reduced demand. Industry would also receive benefits: most allowances would be handed out free (82% in 2012), and billions of dollars of fund money would flow to clean coal and other technology programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal plant owners, coal miners, ratepayers

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on emissions trading, which allows some plants to keep polluting by buying allowances rather than installing controls, and the cap alone does not guarantee cuts at any specific local plant [S2][S3].
More than 80% of allowances in early years would be given free to existing plants rather than auctioned, transferring a valuable new asset to power plant owners and limiting public revenue [S3].

The bill reserves allowance pools and up to 20% of the Climate Action Trust Fund for clean coal technology programs, a subsidy to coal interests, and it gives older plants until 2020 before facing performance standards [S3].

Allowances issued to industry carry real market value, and the offset and early-reduction programs create a complex system whose integrity depends on EPA enforcement to keep credits real and verifiable [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and climate gains are large and the costs fall mainly on the companies responsible for the pollution, though some would pass through to electricity bills. The bill is not pure public policy: it entrenches coal interests with free allowances, clean coal subsidies, and a decade-long runway for the oldest plants. But the design, with rising auction shares and per-ton enforcement, is more protective than prior air bills, and the chief honest objection is that a cap-and-trade system is less certain than direct plant-by-plant rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2007, read twice, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2009, so no committee or floor vote ever took place.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Carper, a Delaware Democrat, introduced the bill on April 20, 2007, joined by original cosponsors including Republicans Sununu, Gregg, and Collins, independents Lieberman, and Democrats Dodd, Feinstein, and Lincoln [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on April 20, 2007; the full action history shows no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of aging coal-fired power plants and the coal industry, which avoided new emission caps, compliance costs, and the requirement that new conventional coal plants go without allowances. Ordinary residents near those plants did not get the promised pollution cuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal plant owners and the coal industry

for.name: Sen. Tom Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort for a four-pollutant cap-and-trade program for power plants.

for.name: 13 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Sununu, Gregg, Dodd, Feinstein, Lincoln, Lieberman, and Collins as original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on April 20, 2007 and took no further action; the bill was never reported out for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start: its 14 Senate backers included 3 Republicans, 1 Independent, and 9 Democrats [S4], and no vote ever occurred to show a partisan divide.

industries.note: The bill caps their sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, mercury, and carbon dioxide emissions and forces eventual performance standards on plants 40 or more years old. It gives them valuable free allowances in early years, but their principal interest in killing the bill ran against the public's interest in cleaner air.

The bill reserves a share of carbon allowances and up to 20% of the trust fund for advanced clean coal technology, subsidizing the industry while conditioning any future conventional coal expansion on those technologies.
A carbon cap raises the value of low- and zero-emitting generation, and the fund supports low- and zero-carbon technology deployment; incremental nuclear generation earns allowances.
New conventional coal plants could not receive carbon allowances, and long-run emission caps would reduce coal demand, though clean coal subsidies soften the blow.
The bill allows agricultural soil sequestration and manure management projects to sell carbon offsets, and farmers share in reforestation and soil programs paid from the auction fund.
